From finding love and securing jobs to pursuing their dreams, Nigerians with Down’s syndrome are defying prejudice and challenging stereotypes to live fulfilling lives. Despite stigma and limited opportunities, they are breaking barriers, showcasing their talents and proving that they, too, deserve the chance to love, work, dream and thrive. IDOWU ABDULLAHI reports Long before Dayo Yahaya’s father began searching for ways to help his son gain independence, it was the infant’s grandmother who first sensed that something was amiss after his birth in July 1996. Amid the family’s joy over the newborn’s arrival in their family home in Kwara State, his grandmother noticed the boy was struggling to gain neck control, a developmental milestone many parents expect infants to reach as they grow. Her observation became an early moment in a journey that would test the family’s understanding and determination in raising a child with Down’s syndrome. “I never knew of the condition then. I had no one to even diagnose it as Down’s syndrome. But my mother saw the signs early through his neck,” Dayo’s father, Usman Yahaya, told PUNCH Healthwise. It was until the family welcomed their third child that they had to face the reality that Dayo was different. “Till we had the third child years later, he didn’t crawl; he was just moving about using his chest like a snake,” Yahaya said. Hidden from the world When Dayo’s developmental delays became impossible to ignore, his family’s initial hope gradually gave way to the realities of societal stigma. With Nigeria’s unique culture where physical and neurological conditions are frequently misunderstood, the young boy was quietly hidden from the public. “When we saw the third-born was picking up, whenever we had visitors coming in, we always hurriedly took him away from the parlour to hide him in the bedroom,” Yahaya told PUNCH Healthwise. While Dayo was hidden from the community around him, the family had no choice but to enroll him in school like children of school age. Enrolled in a school unequipped to accommodate his needs, he couldn’t catch up with what was being taught in class. Amid this, it was Dayo’s grandma who cared for him and gave him more sense of belonging. “When his grandma died, there was a shift in me. I realised I had to stop hiding him and treat him like my other children. When I noticed he was always repeating class, one day, I just decided to let him learn handiwork. I enrolled him to learn barbering,” Yahaya said. While Yahaya, who is a retired Director at the Kwara State Local Government Commission, quickly accepted his son as a special kid after his grandma passed away, many parents of children with DS in Nigeria struggle to overcome the stigma. Welcoming a newborn usually brings joy, but a Down’s syndrome diagnosis can instantly turn that celebration into heartbreak for unprepared parents. For many families, the heavy emotional and financial toll of raising a child with special needs remains overwhelming. What is Down syndrome? Down’s syndrome is a genetic condition caused by the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21. Most people have 46 chromosomes in their cells, while people with Down syndrome usually have 47. According to the United States National Institute of Child Health and Human Development, the extra chromosome results from a random error in cell division in most cases. It added that the condition is not caused by anything a parent did or failed to do during pregnancy. There are three types of Down’s syndrome known as Trisomy 21, Mosaicism, and Translocation, experts say. The condition can affect physical development, learning, communication, and the acquisition of everyday skills of persons living with it. Some persons with DS also have associated medical conditions, including congenital heart defects, hearing or vision problems, and thyroid disorders. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, mothers aged 35 and older are more at risk of having a baby with DS than younger mothers. The probability increases the older the mother is, CDC says. Similarly, a 2003 study published by Columbia University Irving Medical Center found that fathers over 40 had twice the chance of having a child with Down syndrome. However, speaking with PUNCH Healthwise, a professor of pediatrics, Aminu Mohammed, explained that babies with DS typically have a few distinguishing characteristics from birth. He listed the characteristics to include flat facial features, a small head, a short neck, a protruding tongue, eyes that slant upward, strangely shaped ears, and low muscle tone. He added that people with DS are at higher risk of health conditions, which include: congenital heart defects, hearing loss, poor vision, cataracts, leukemia, chronic constipation, sleep apnea, dementia, hypothyroidism, and obesity. “With regular health surveillance, early intervention, therapies (physiotherapy, speech therapy), and cardiac care when needed, many children with Down’s syndrome grow up healthy and lead fulfilling lives,” Mohammed said. According to the United Nations, the estimated incidence of DS is between 1 in 1,000 and 1 in 1,100 live births worldwide. Each year, approximately 3,000 to 5,000 children are born with this chromosome disorder. One out of 865 live births in Nigeria over nine years was born with Down Syndrome, according to a study on the incidence of DS in Nigeria. Each year, an estimated 3,000 to 5,000 children are born with this chromosome disorder in the country. Defying odds While others questioned Dayo’s abilities, his father was determined to give him the chance to learn, practise and become more independent. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. When Yahaya was repeatedly investing in Dayo, he faced criticism from people who doubted that the young man could achieve much because he was living with Down syndrome. “After I noticed his interest in driving and fast learning in driving school, I bought him a car in 2014. Some of my friends also criticised me. “They said I was wasting money by spending it on a child they believed had little or no hope of achieving anything. They wondered why I was buying a car for him and investing so much in him,” Yahaya recalled. Despite the criticism, he said he continued to create opportunities for him by encouraging him to cycle, play table tennis, and other activities that helped improve his coordination, participate in everyday life, and ensure Dayo was recognised as an individual beyond his diagnosis. In 2018, he said the family’s encounters with the Down Syndrome Foundation Nigeria introduced Dayo to the world. “In 2019, Dayo was in Lagos for a DSFN programme where persons living with Down syndrome were showcasing their talents and skills. It was there he showed his driving skills, and that announced him to the world. “From there, we got to know about the National Down Syndrome Congress in the US. We were invited to the University of Pennsylvania, where Dayo showcased his talents. “So, it later became a yearly thing, and we attended several other congresses. In fact, it was Dayo, through his talents, that exposed me to the world,” he said. Marital journey With Dayo’s experience in the US and sheer activeness around female peers, Yahaya decided to get his son married. In 2020, Dayo got married to a typical lady. The marriage was another step towards challenging assumptions about what people living with the condition could achieve. “While we were in the US, I had approached a parent whose daughter Dayo took a liking to, who is also living with Down’s syndrome. Her father told us he couldn’t decide for her, as they don’t know if the daughter would later want to have a male or female as a partner. “When we got back to Nigeria, I had to get him a lady to marry. He married someone who is not living with the condition. Before the marriage, I had paired him with a lady and confirmed he could have sexual intercourse. So, he’s married,” Yahaya, who is the Director and Chairman, Board of Trustees, Down Syndrome Skills Acquisition Centre, Ilorin, said. Govt’s employment Yahaya said his son, who is now 30 years old, got a job at a Federal Government facility in Kwara. “We visited the Federal Neuropsychiatric Hospital, Budo-Egba, Kwara State over a health issue in March 2026. “I told them about his (Dayo’s) abilities and certificates. They were impressed. The medical director asked me whether I could provide the certificate he had from his barbering and other skills. “He told me to bring it (certificates) because they had a department, the occupational therapy department, where they trained admitted patients in handwork, and Dayo’s skills and talents could become useful. “That was how Dayo was employed at the hospital, which is just a 10-minute drive from my house. He was employed there as an occupational therapy attendant on CONHESS 3 step 2,” he said. Reflecting on his son’s progress, Yahaya urged other parents to focus on helping their children acquire practical skills that could support their livelihoods. “So, I want to advise parents to get their children or wards living with Down syndrome to learn different skills,” he said. With a series of screenings and tests, healthcare professionals can detect Down’s syndrome before or after birth. Down’s syndrome can affect a person’s cognitive ability and physical growth, causing mild to moderate developmental issues. But these differences matter in a society where a diagnosis can become a lifelong label, overshadowing those living with the condition’s interests and potential. Medical experts say early identification and intervention can make a difference in supporting children with DS. The Head of Paediatrics at the Federal Teaching Hospital, Katsina, Dr Abdurrazzaq Alege, said that depending on their individual needs, people living with DS may benefit from regular medical assessments, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language support, and specialised educational services. The child health expert said these interventions can help them develop communication, movement and everyday living skills. “For parents of children with Down syndrome, my advice is that their baby is special and, therefore, requires special needs. If this is done appropriately, it is going to give the child a very good life, and the parents will have no reason to regret bringing the child into the world. “There are network groups and social groups for these children. Part of what these children need is therapy. Once mothers or parents see other children with similar conditions, they tend to have greater peace of mind. So, we advise them to join these groups and take advantage of whatever new interventions or other measures are available to them. “These children may not be able to attend a regular school, but there are schools specifically for children with these needs that they can attend, so that their education can be tailored to their needs. “These interventions, including training, sometimes have to be tailored to the child’s needs. So, it may not necessarily be academics alone. It could also involve skills acquisition. All these are ways of helping the child develop and achieve something in life,” Alege said. Unique abilities In 1990, when the Omere family welcomed their fifth child, Solomon Omere, their joy knew no bounds. Solomon’s mother, Eugenia Omere, who was a professional nurse, observed his delayed speech development and developmental milestones at 18 months, after which a paediatrician diagnosed him with DS. Despite being tutored by special needs teachers since three years old, Solomon was enrolled at a primary school in Akoka, Lagos State, where he later struggled academically which prevented him from proceeding to secondary school. In 2023, Mrs Omere enrolled Solomon at Down Syndrome Foundation Nigeria in a bid to ensure his son got the needed help to unlock his potential, a move which later paid off. “I was introduced to sporting activities such as basketball, boxing, and choreography. I joined the school’s basketball team. “In 2015, I was part of 42 athletes who represented Nigeria at the Special Olympics World Summer Games in Los Angeles, United States. The team came second, and I won a silver medal at the Olympics,” Solomon told PUNCH Healthwise. Now 35, Solomon, who is from Edo State, said that despite enjoying sporting activities, he has also pursued an interest in baking and acting. His talent has also earned him a place in a popular Nigerian movie series, Godwin, in 2014. The series was directed and produced by Wale Adenuga Productions. “I was the main character in Godwin,” he said. While still with DSFN, Solomon now inspires others living with DS, and he’s currently employed by the foundation. Advocacy champion At 26, Moyosore Ijale is determined to ensure that people living with DS and other disabilities are heard, respected, and included in decisions affecting their lives. Rather than allow others to speak on their behalf, he is championing self-advocacy, encouraging people with DS to understand their rights and demand equal opportunities. “I’m a self-advocate. I lead others, and I’m a good leader. I want to ensure everyone comes together and we can advocate for ourselves and demand better from the government,” Moyosore told PUNCH Healthwise. Moyosore said he was committed to exploring opportunities that enable people with disabilities to participate meaningfully in society. According to him, inclusion must translate into equal rights, opportunities and the freedom to determine their own futures. He added, “I speak for myself and others on our rights as persons with disabilities. We have rights to life, marriage, education, and healthcare services. “I want to advocate for our rights in society, because we have employment rights, and people should not see us as persons with disabilities alone, but see us as normal people who can equally perform any task,” she said. Moyosore’s father, Olayinka Ijale, said they were able to recognise the DS sign in him when he was three weeks old. With that knowledge, he said they were able to get him the needed interventions early. The early interventions, he said, were the game changer for Moyosore, who is now a proud self-advocate. “I was able to understand his condition right from the beginning after his diagnosis. My wife and I discussed what was best to do for his development, and we were able to guide him along. “My wife and I discussed what was best to do for his development, which really helped him build skills before he eventually transitioned to DSFN,” Mr Ijale told PUNCH Healthwise. Five-time Olympics gold medallist Beyond the assumptions often associated with DS, Adedamola Roberts used sport as an avenue to demonstrate his abilities and build a successful public identity. Roberts, born in Lagos to a medical doctor couple, Seyi and Alero Roberts, schooled at Corona School, Victoria Island, Lagos, before going to the Children’s Developmental Centre. It was at the centre that his sporting career took off. Roberts later defied the odds of DS by becoming a five-time Special Olympics gold medallist as a swimmer. He won gold medals in Los Angeles 2015, Greece 2011, Ireland 2003 and Abu Dhabi [bronze] in 2019. Roberts recalled representing Nigeria in athletics in Ireland in 2003. Although he finished first in his event, he was disqualified for crossing into another lane. Despite his disqualification, he rose to the occasion and later became a celebrated swimmer with laurels to show for it. “I intend to continue demonstrating the infinite opportunities of sports in different abilities and preaching the gospel of inclusivity and equality in diversity. Truth is, even though we’re all different, we’re all the same. “We all bleed red and need oxygen and water to survive. Our differences need to strengthen us collectively, not divide us. I want to bring that gospel of inclusivity down to earth, and translate it into practical things people and corporate bodies can do to improve the lot of others and increase their social value,” Roberts, who is now 41, told PUNCH in 2019. What parents should do Meanwhile, parents of persons living with DS have been urged to accept their children’s condition, seek early intervention and provide the support needed to help them develop their abilities and live fulfilling lives. The DSFN Vice Chairman, Parents Teachers’ Association, Olayinka Ijale, stressed that a diagnosis should not be seen as the end of a child’s prospects, noting that appropriate care, education and family support could improve their development and independence. He urged parents to seek professional guidance and enrol their children in appropriate educational and developmental programmes, rather than hide them because of stigma or misconceptions about the condition. According to him, persons with DS have different abilities and support needs, making it important for parents to understand their individual strengths and challenges. “Individuals with Down’s syndrome may take things slow, but with the right support, learning, and patience, they will get there. “If you are quick to accept that your child has Down’s syndrome, you will be able to manage it. There is still a general societal stigma surrounding it, but it demands continuous care unless,” he said. He added, “I want to advise every parent out there who has a child living with Down syndrome: please do not neglect them. God has a reason for creating them the way they are. Nobody can create a human being without God’s knowledge. “Take them to special schools where their future can be nurtured. Do not hide them. Many parents lock their children in a room whenever they have visitors or functions, and that is very wrong,” Ijale said. Stakeholders demand right policies Meanwhile, stakeholders have called on the government to implement policies that protect the rights of people living with DS and promote their inclusion in education, healthcare, employment and other aspects of society. The Chief Executive Officer of DSFN, Mrs. Rose Mordi, said governments at all levels need to put deliberate measures in place to ensure persons with the condition have equal opportunities to develop their abilities and participate meaningfully in their communities. According to her, the absence of effective implementation of inclusive policies could further expose them to exclusion. “It is the responsibility of the government to put structures in place to take care of these children and create awareness to demystify the condition. But because that has not been done, it becomes a big challenge. As a result, many of these families hide their children away, or abandon them,” she said. Mordi, whose foundation recently celebrated its 25th anniversary, listed priority areas the government should focus on to ensure inclusion for persons living with DS. She said, “The first is policy change. There has to be a structure, the right structure, put in place for them. You see, when we talk about disability, there are disabilities, and there are disabilities. Even within the disability sector, there is still discrimination. “I’m sure you can attest to the fact that people with visual impairments are being offered employment. People with hearing impairments get employed. People who use wheelchairs get employed, but it is not so with people living with Down syndrome. The government must ensure persons with Down syndrome and other intellectual disabilities are properly captured in all the provisions that are put in place. “Secondly, there should be a lot of advocacy. The government should encourage this. We should collaborate with government agencies to carry out vigorous advocacy, awareness creation, and enlightenment, especially in rural areas, about the condition. “Thirdly, people living with Down’s syndrome should be properly trained and given their rightful position in society by being employed. First of all, they cannot be employed if they are not trained, and this has not happened. It has not been happening, and that is one of the things the foundation has been advocating for over the years.” Idowu Abdullahi
